Littler has long talked about his hope of completing the clean sweep of majors in 2026, which hinged on a triumph in Blackpool. He completed that triumph and then some with a record-breaking 18-9 win over Gerwyn Price, setting a new record average in a final of 111.53.

He also broke his own record for the number of 180s hit across the tournament, improving his 64 in 2025 to 66 in 2026.

The victory in Blackpool saw Littler become only the fourth player in tournament history to win back-to-back titles, and the first in a decade to achieve the feat.

It was not just his performance in the final that astounded. He averaged over 109 against Niko Springer, backed that up with a 113 average plus a nine-darter against Nathan Aspinall, averaged 109 again against Josh Rock, then demolished Dirk van Duijvenbode to get into the big dance once again.

It was pure darting dominance.

Now, he has his sights set on racking up major after major to ensure not just that he holds them all, but he holds them all in one calendar year.

In 2026, he has won the World Darts Championship, UK Open, Premier League, Masters, and now the Matchplay.

So what is up next?

Well, instead of a holiday to Spain, he will head off to Leicester...

What does he need to do on the Pro Tours?

As part of the clean sweep, Littler will have to defend his Players Championship Finals win in Minehead at the end of November.

However, he has not yet qualified for that tournament.

Littler currently sits £22,500 off qualification and there are 10 Players Championship events remaining in 2026.

The world No 1 has ruled out heading to Hildesheim on July 28 and 29 which means his next opportunity to try and secure qualification will come on August 25 and 26 at Players Championship 27 and 28 in Leicester.

There are then two more events in Leicester on November 4 and 5 with Littler indicating that he is likely to use these four to try and qualify.

Based on 2025, plus factoring in the increased prize money, the projected cut-off looks to be around £30,000.

At each event, there is £15,000 on offer for a title, with £10,000 for the runner up and £6,500 for a semi-final.

Taking all that into account, it looks like Littler would need to win at least one final and make another final but there is a scenario in which he may need to win a couple of these events.

Of course, what other players achieve at the remaining 10 events all will get factored in but Littler will know at least one victory and a good run is required.

World Series of Darts Finals

The next job on the list for Littler is the World Series of Darts Finals in Amsterdam on September 17-20.

Littler came within one victory of retaining his title after losing out to Michael van Gerwen in Amsterdam in 2025.

The previous year he won the tournament by beating Michael Smith 11-4.

Then back to Leicester... for the World Grand Prix!

The next PDC-ranked TV major is the BoyleSports World Grand Prix from September 28 - October 4 at the Mattioli Arena, Leicester, live on Sky Sports.

Littler returns as defending champion after last year's victory over Luke Humphries in the double in, double out event.

By this stage, Littler will have attended two of his Players Championship events so will know how close he is to Minehead qualification.

The one he is missing: European Championship

There is also one major alluding Littler in his collection at the moment, the European Championship, which takes place on October 22-25 in Dortmund.

Gian van Veen stunned Humphries in a dramatic 11-10 victory to claim the first major trophy of his career in 2025.

Littler, meanwhile, bowed out at the last-16 stage in a 10-7 win over James Wade.

Wolverhampton up next!

By the time Littler heads to Wolverhampton for the Grand Slam of Darts on November 14-22, live on Sky Sports, he will have had all his opportunities to qualify for the Players Championship Finals.

Littler went back-to-back at the Grand Slam with an imperious 16-11 win over Humphries.

Making it three in a row is the next requirement to continue his target.

More magic in Minehead?

If Littler has done what he needs to on the Pro Tour, then a trip to Minehead on November 27-29 is the penultimate piece of the puzzle.

Littler secured a win in 2025 with an 11-8 victory over Nathan Aspinall in the final.

If 'The Nuke' backs up at Minehead, after completing the ridiculous list above, then there is just one more task.

Three in a row at Ally Pally...

How Littler would love to make it three in a row on darts' biggest stage in order to complete the season haul and run into 2027 with back-to-back clean sweeps in his sights.

In 2025, he beat Van Gerwen. In 2026, he beat Van Veen.

If he were to cap off a spectacular year in the most spectacular of fashions, he would become the first person since Phil Taylor in 2006 to win the title three times on the spin.

"I have always said, I have got to win 16 Matchplays, 16 worlds, and then have a look at whatever else Phil Taylor did win," Littler said.

An unprecedented trophy haul would be a good start.

articles.title: Luke Littler: Target Darts explain the science behind World No 1's phenomenal success
articles.summary: "He's back-to-back world champion, what he could do in the sport is entirely up to him" - James Tattersall, CEO of Target Darts, says the world is Luke Littler's oyster; you can watch the BoyleSports World Grand Prix live on Sky Sports from Sept 28 to Oct 4 in Leicester
articles.body:
Want to know the secret behind the success of darting phenom Luke Littler?

Littler has spearheaded darts' surge towards the mainstream since he broke on the scene with his debut run to the 2024 World Championship final as a 16-year-old.

Darts manufacturer Target Darts has supported the global superstar since the age of 12. In February 2024, the teenager signed a multi-year mega-deal reported to be worth up to £20 million - the most lucrative the sport has ever seen.

  • Luke Littler dominates Gerwyn Price to close out historic World Matchplay defence
  • Darts in 2026: Key dates, calendar, results 📅
  • Got Sky? Watch on the Sky Sports app 📱
  • Not got Sky? Get instant access with NOW 📺

Littler possesses a generational talent when it comes to playing darts and Sky Sports pundit Wayne Mardle has said "he's probably the most natural naturally gifted player I've ever seen in my life".

Since the moment the Warrington-born star first held a dart, he's become a record-breaker and history-maker.

James Tattersall, CEO of Target Darts, says both the company and Littler are "aligned" in where they want to see the future of darts go.

Speaking at an event in which Target have set out a vision to inspire 100 million people to play darts by the end of the decade, he explained the process of how Littler sat down with chairman Garry Plummer, the design team, and engineers to build darts to perfect his game.

"I think some of the inspiration was drawn from Adrian Lewis' darts and the pixel grip, which is a unique grip that Target has and that worked its way into building up Luke's original G1," said Tattersall. "That was the barrel, but over the years Luke's tweaked it and challenged us to improve it. The point length has changed, the shaft and flight have changed to a K-Flex system before his first World Championships."

F-Flex is a one-piece flight and shaft innovation that screws into the back of the barrel.

Tattersall explained: "What it helps you do is when you're throwing darts together in such tight groupings like Luke does, the thing you want to avoid is that dart coming in and deflecting off the dart that's already in the board and the K-Flex helps reduce those deflections substantially.

"And longer points - it's like the balance of the dart and how it flies and how it lands through the air. I think another part of it is it keeps the barrel section of the dart further away from the treble and that creates more space in the board."

Talent vs Equipment?

"His talent is all down to him," says Tattersall. "I think when you're talking about the equipment, we're talking about making Luke comfortable with all of that talent and giving him the right equipment that he's confident with to use and just to get those last few percentages, but Luke's an extraordinary player regardless."

With two world titles in three visits to Alexandra Palace, and 14 major titles to his name, Littler is well on his way to joining Phil Taylor as a legend of the sport.

The problem for his rivals is that he is still getting better after the Warrington star crushed Gerwyn Price 18-9 to retain his Betfred World Matchplay title in Blackpool on Sunday.

Littler was in imperious form as he set a new record for the final with an average of 111.53, lifting his average for the tournament as a whole to 111.04 to break Phil Taylor's previous high mark of 106.31.

The win keeps Littler on course for a clean sweep of trophies in 2026 having already won the World Championship, UK Open, Premier League and the Masters.

The supporting cast behind Littler

Littler's management have invested in sports psychologists, nutritionists, performance coaches, and biomechanics in order to get the most out of their talent, and the teenager has benefitted in every area to help support his game.

"Mentality is absolutely key. We want to protect the players. The stage is lonely up there, and darts is a gruelling sport," Tattersall said.

"It's a bit like a penalty shootout, but every single time you're throwing a dart. It's such a closed skill, and it's so repetitive. Your mindset's got to be really, really clear, and you get those big momentum swings, you think you're about to checkout the double, you miss by a millimetre, your opponent throws in a big 170 checkout, and that's a punch in the stomach. It's how do you recover from that for the next leg? That's sports psychology, and it's crucial in all sports. I don't know why it's a surprise that it should not be in darts."

'We want to learn about action - not create robots'

With biomechanics, the cameras observe how a player throws darts, with sports science data helping ways of working on the technique in order to improve.

Target have ideas but Tattersall insists implementing them will not turn the Luke Littlers of this world into robots.

"That's the last thing we want to do," he said. "What we want to do is discover and learn about the sport, and learn about that action, because why is it that there are different throwing techniques?

"If you look at something like golf, where you know suddenly you come along with the Vardon grip [or overlapping grip], and that becomes almost the only way to hold a golf club.

"I think the high jump has got that really famous example of how the sport, science, innovated, [Fosbury flop], you ended up with that kind of one technique point.

"I think there will always be different ways of throwing a dart, and there will be different ways of improving those different styles, and maybe that particular style is because you're tall, and maybe that particular style is because you've got longer arms, we don't know yet, but that's what we're going to find out, and then use that data accordingly."

Zoe Burton, Chief Transformation Officer at Target Darts, says Littler is already inspiring the next generation with his natural talent, although the company are slowly moving towards a performance technology system, which is currently being tested on a number of players.

"If you look at a young person and you think of their journey as they get into a sport, you need an inspiring player - that person who they look up to - and can almost aspire to be. Luke Littler provides that," said Buton.

"You need a natural talent, but that gets you so far. Then it's determination and I think psychology as well.

"What makes a star player become a great and world-class player is actually their ability to focus under pressure and make those doubles It's never going to be robotic."

articles.title: Commonwealth Games: Adam Ramsay-Peaty's emotional reaction to bronze medals shows event still matters, says Laura Kenny
articles.summary: Dame Laura Kenny admits Adam Ramsay-Peaty should have acknowledged his competitors after bronze medal wins, but six-time Olympic medallist says emotional interviews show importance of Commonwealth Games
articles.body:
Adam Ramsay-Peaty's emotional reaction to his Commonwealth Games performances has illustrated just how important the event is to athletes, according to Dame Laura Kenny.

Three-time Olympic swimming champion Ramsay-Peaty was visibly tearful after picking up two bronze medals at this summer's downsized tournament, first in the 100m breaststroke and then again in the 50m.

After previously going eight years unbeaten in the 100m, Ramsay-Peaty was clearly disappointed with his performance, admitting "nothing makes sense" in interviews afterwards.

  • Commonwealth Games Glasgow 2026 LIVE

  • Not got Sky? Get Sky Sports or stream with no contract on NOW📺

The 31-year-old's takes have received a mixed reception from fans watching on - but now-retired six-time medal-winning Olympic cyclist Kenny believes Ramsay-Peaty showed "strength" to show up under "a lot of pressure."

"He was emotional after the first one and obviously to bring yourself back round, to come back up and perform the way he did for a bronze medal, that takes strength in itself," Kenny told Sky Sports News.

"The emotion that he showed in those interviews post-bronze just shows how much the Commonwealth Games means to these athletes.

"You're performing under the pressure, you're coming back from ultimately being a superhero and held to such a high standard that people almost expect you to win gold every single time.

"Coming from someone who has experienced that, the pressure of that can be a lot. You're under the spotlight for two weeks every two years and that is a lot of pressure to have to deal with.

"Throw into the mix stuff that has or hasn't happened in his personal life, I think it is a lot for you then to come out and perform."

Ramsay-Peaty has recently vowed to let his swimming do the talking following his high-profile wedding to Holly Ramsay, daughter of chef Gordon Ramsay, and a subsequent family fallout.

He also drew criticism for a failure to congratulate his fellow athletes in his interviews after his bronze finishes.

Kenny understands the negative reaction to Ramsay-Peaty's comments at the Glasgow Games.

"I probably would have started with saying well done to the athletes that got gold and silver," she said.

"But I can totally understand because, in the heat of the moment, when you are getting asked questions immediately after you've performed, it's so emotional, anything comes out."

These Games were originally scheduled to take place in Victoria, Australia, but the organisers pulled out due to spiralling costs, with Glasgow stepping in to pick up hosting duties.

After going ahead with just 10 sports, there have been fears for the future of the event, but Kenny believes it remains important.

"Athletes want to compete," Kenny, who retired in 2024, said. "For me, taking away the Commonwealth Games would have been one last chance to compete. It would have been one less multi-sport event that we had on the calendar.

"The Commonwealth Games is one of the only times para-athletes and able-bodied athletes coincide, so why would we take that away? It's also got the added element that the home nations are split up, so actually it's really nice to compete for Team England.

"You've got all these National Lottery funded athletes that ultimately want to train and race and compete, so why would we want that off the calendar?"

articles.title: F1 season to end in Europe if Qatar, Abu Dhabi unable to host due to war
articles.summary: F1 sets a mid-September deadline to decide whether final rounds in Middle East can be held due to US-Israel war on Iran.
articles.body:
Formula One will ⁠end the season in Europe ⁠if races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi cannot be held and has set a mid-September deadline, the Liberty Media-owned sport’s Chief Executive Stefano Domenicali has said.

“We will take the maximum time for us to see how the situation will develop and we will take the decision at the right time,” Domenicali told reporters on Wednesday.

Races scheduled for Saudi Arabia and Bahrain ⁠in April were called off due to the US-Israel war on Iran, with Malaysia’s Sepang circuit now due to host the latter on October 4, with the Gulf kingdom paying most of the costs.

The FIA-sanctioned World Endurance Championship (WEC) has already moved its ⁠last two rounds in Qatar and Bahrain to Barcelona’s Circuit de Catalunya and Italy’s Monza in October and November.

Domenicali said, “The deadline for the decision of any possible change of the actual calendar is the middle of September.”

“For us ‌today, the races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi are confirmed. By the way, they are already sold out,” he added. “If this will not be possible, the end of the season will be in Europe because we cannot go in other places.”

Qatar is due to host F1 on November 29 and Abu Dhabi in the United Arab Emirates on December 6.

Domenicali confirmed Italy’s Imola circuit, his birthplace and home to Ferrari as well as Mercedes’s Formula One leader Kimi Antonelli, was on the list of possible replacements.

Informed sources have touted Imola, dropped from the calendar ⁠this year, as a leading candidate despite the weather at that time of year.

Domenicali said ⁠the temperatures in the US city of Las Vegas during the Saturday night race in November were colder than in Europe.

“There was a possibility of having two races in Las Vegas [to end the season] but we don’t want to ruin a jewel that is growing,” he said, adding that there would also be ⁠added competition with the regular NFL season.

The 2027 calendar has yet to be published, but Bahrain was expected, before the conflict erupted, to take back its slot as season-opener ⁠⁠from Australia in March.

The Italian said Formula One planned to publish a schedule ⁠later in the year.

“Of course, in case the situation in the Middle East would not be solved, we have options, different plans,” Domenicali said. “But the trigger for that, of course, is at the end of the year. So we still have a lot of time.”

“We will keep, in any ‌case, the target of 24 grands prix also for next year.”

Portugal and Turkiye will return as new rounds on the calendar next year, Domenicali said. Longer term, there were positive negotiations with possible hosts in Africa and interest from ‌Asia ‌and South America.

“We have more requests in China and Japan, but for the moment we want to stay with one race in China because we need to consolidate the market before thinking to have another option there,” he added.

articles.title: Players Championship 26: Sebastian Bialecki claims second PDC ranking title as Henry Coates and Beau Greaves shine
articles.summary: Sebastian Bialecki picked up his second PDC ranking title, one year on from winning his first; Beau Greaves averaged 106 and 104 in a strong showing; watch the BoyleSports World Grand Prix live on Sky Sports from Sept 28 to Oct 4 in Leicester
articles.body:
Sebastian Bialecki secured his second PDC ranking title with a hard-fought 8-6 victory against Mario Vandenbogaerde in Wednesday's Players Championship 26 final.

Exactly a year to the day since he claimed his maiden ranking title in Hildesheim, Bialecki repeated the feat on German soil, overturning a 5-3 deficit to cap off another memorable triumph.

The 22-year-old has celebrated an astonishing six Development Tour titles in 2026, and he reaffirmed his credentials by returning to the winner's circle at Halle 39.

Bialecki began his title challenge with successive ton-plus averages in deciding-leg wins over Dennie Olde Kalter and Cor Dekker, recovering from 5-3 down in his opener against Olde Kalter.

However, Poland's No 2 then conceded just three legs in his next three matches, dispatching Viktor Tingstrom, Bradley Brooks and Damon Heta to storm through to the semi-finals.

Bialecki reeled off five consecutive legs from 4-2 down to dump out European Champion Gian van Veen in the last four, before displaying similar resistance against Belgian veteran Vandenbogaerde.

Vandenbogaerde led 3-1 and 5-3 at one stage, but Bialecki delivered a timely mid-match burst, converting consecutive 101 and 100 checkouts and winning five of the last six legs to prevail.

"I don't know what I can say. It's an unbelievable feeling," reflected Bialecki, who currently occupies eighth spot on the Players Championship rankings.

"Before this tournament, I saw on my Facebook memories that it was the day I won my first one [title] a year ago.

"Maybe this tournament was a little bit similar, because I also won the first match from 3-5 down. I'm over the moon now."

Bialecki's second ProTour title puts him firmly in contention for a place in the upcoming World Grand Prix, which takes place in Leicester from September 28-October 4, live on Sky Sports.

Elsewhere, Monday's champion Henry Coates continued his groundbreaking week in Hildesheim, averaging 109.34 and 105.79 prior to his defeat against Justin Hood.

Newly crowned Women's World Matchplay champion Beau Greaves also averaged north of 106 and 104 in victories over Adam Paxton and Yorick Hofkens respectively, before succumbing to a resurgent Damon Heta.

Earlier in the day, Scott Williams produced perfection during his opening round success against Callan Rydz, although his hopes of a significant run were also thwarted by Heta in round two.

articles.title: Luke Littler edges Scottie Scheffler and Jannik Sinner as the 'most dominant sportsperson' - Love The Darts podcast
articles.summary: After Luke Littler's dominant World Matchplay victory, Laura Turner and Chris Murphy debate on the Love The Darts podcast whether 'The Nuke' is the most dominant sportsperson in the world right now
articles.body:
Teenage dart sensation Luke Littler has left the darts world questioning if anyone will ever get near him again after winning the World Matchplay Darts on Sunday.

'The Nuke' stormed to victory in Blackpool, winning the competition for the second year in a row and seeing off final opponent Gerwyn Price 18-9.

Littler being in total control at a darts competition is nothing new. He's won every PDC major title in 2026 so far, and his World Matchplay performance has made it very difficult to argue he's not head and shoulders above his competitors.

  • Not got Sky? Get Sky Sports or stream with no contract on NOW📺

His mind-blowing performances have sparked debate over where he ranks in the sporting world, leading Sky Sports' Love The Darts podcast pundits, former darts player Laura Turner and darts commentator Chris Murphy, to debate whether he is indeed the most dominant sportsperson in the world right now.

"It's a very difficult question, how do you measure dominance?" Murphy said. "Darts seems to have more majors than any other sport, if you're doing it on major titles, but then again if you just took the top four and made it fair, he wins what you might call the Grand Slam titles.

"He holds them all and he's on course to have a clean sweep of every title so of course he does. I think yes [he is the most dominant]."

Murphy then named two other sporting stars that come close to giving Littler a run for his money - tennis world No 1 Jannik Sinner and his golf equivalent, Scottie Scheffler - but concluded neither can touch him.

"Looking at other sports, we've mentioned tennis, Sinner maybe he's in the conversation," he said. "Scheffler in golf has been No 1 for a long time, but I don't think any of them get near Littler."

Turner agreed, pointing out how rare it is to have two English people dominating a sport in both the men's and women's editions at the same time.

"It's very hard to say no [he isn't the most dominant] isn't it," Turner said. "From a women's darts point of view actually I think [Women's World Matchplay winner] Beau Greaves is unbelievably dominant, she's just picked up the Matchplay in Blackpool. She won 17 out of the 24 titles available in that qualification process as well.

"She's been on a run of 114 consecutive wins, it took Fallon [Sherrock] at a 102 average just to stop that run. Beau is very dominant.

"In darts at the moment I personally think we're very lucky, I know Beau is on the Pro Tour as well. I can't think of another sport where at this moment in time, anyone that is dominating in the way they are."

Does Littler edge Taylor as darts' greatest?

While Turner and Murphy have been wowed by Littler this month, they believe the teenager still has a while to go until he can call himself darts' greatest ever.

Asked if he is the best darts player to ever do it, Murphy replied: "No, and this is where I think we need to zoom out a little bit. Potential to best the greatest? Possibly, but I don't think it's especially close yet to be honest.

"It's not criticism of his abilities and talents, it's just simple arithmetic I suppose. Phil Taylor's title tally, 16 world titles, spanning across four different generations of darts players, and he's had to reinvent himself for different games in different eras."

Taylor, who retired in 2018, holds the record for the most darts world titles. Littler, meanwhile, has two, winning the PDC World Darts Championship in 2025 and 2026 after bursting on the scene in 2024.

Laura agreed that Littler has a way to go yet to edge Taylor, adding: "All of us suffer from recency bias. There's a lot of people don't forget that never engaged in darts to the level they are before Luke Littler came onto the scene.

"Ultimately, Phil has played through different generations, I don't want to say mind games but you know you can get under people's skin a bit more.

"Ability wise, and all the accolades he has won over all those years, you have to say Phil is the greatest ever darts player we've had.

"Luke Littler perhaps one of the most dominant sports people at this time."

articles.summary: WNBA basketball team Seattle Storm apologize after co-owner berates girls with ‘thank you’ sign for Sophie Cunningham.
articles.body:
The Seattle Storm has issued an apology statement, one day after one of their co-owners verbally accosted two teenage female fans ⁠with expletives because they ⁠were holding signs supporting the views of Indiana’s Sophie Cunningham during a home game against the Fever.

The teenagers each had a sign, one saying “Thank You Sophie ⁠for speaking up for girls!” Cunningham recently went to bat for the protection of women’s sports and keeping them female only.

Independent journalist Brandi Kruse reported that minority owner Celeste Keaton told the girls ⁠they were “f—ing insane”.

“We are aware one of our co-owners made comments to two fans in attendance at last night’s game,” Storm majority owner Ginny Gilder said in a statement on Wednesday.

“We apologize that this happened. Everyone who attends a Storm game deserves to feel welcome, and we remain committed to creating an ‌inclusive environment where every fan is treated with respect.”

Kruse told Fox News that the scene included Seattle players making thumbs-down gestures to the girls. Some fans also made their opinions known.

“Some of the fans were relentlessly booing at them,” Kruse told Fox News. “And I kind of turned around and said, ‘Look, they’re just teenage girls.'”

Last year, a New York Times poll suggested that 79% of Americans don’t want men playing in women’s sports.

The issue was recently ⁠in the news when the Supreme Court issued a ruling in June ⁠that states can ban transgender athletes from participating in women’s and girls’ sports.

During a recent interview with ESPN, Cunningham weighed in about women’s sports, emphasising girls should never have to compete with biological men.

“I got a lot of ⁠negative feedback about me hating trans,” Cunningham told ESPN. “And I’m like, ‘I never once said that.’

“I think that I am here to extend love. ⁠But I also think with that love is truth, being ⁠honest. And I want to protect young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn’t have to go against biological men.”

Cunningham received a mix of cheers and jeers during Wednesday’s game, which was won 105-95 by ‌the Fever. There was a rally outside the arena before the game, where proponents of women’s sports had signs thanking Cunningham for speaking up for girls and women. Pro-transgender activists were also on the scene.

The Fever did not allow Cunningham to face questions after the game. She made three 3-pointers and scored 11 points.

The Storm (6-24) lost their seventh straight game and own the worst record in the league.

articles.title: Luke Littler insists 'clean sweep very much on' as he attends Warrington mural unveiling days after World Matchplay win

Luke Littler believes "not many" can stop him in the form he showed at the World Matchplay as he sets his sights on a 2026 majors clean sweep.

The 2026 PDC World Championship winner was frightenedly good in Blackpool, beating darts legend Phil Taylor's Matchplay record average of 106.31 with 111.04.

"I'm feeling very good," Littler told Sky Sports at the unveiling of his mural in Warrington on Thursday. "With performances like that, not many can stop me. Obviously, a tournament average of 111 was really, really good."

As it stands, he could still achieve an unprecedented clean sweep of eight ranking titles in the calendar - and Littler admitted that record is on his mind going forward, starting with working on qualifying to defend his Players Championship Finals title.

"The clean sweep is very much on," he said. "I think you can only look at what's coming up. For myself now, I can't go and say 'I'm going to win the World Championships'. That's in another five or six months.

"For darts, I think it would be up there with probably one of the best," he said. "No one's ever done it. That's what I'm going for. I like to break all these records."

Littler's mural was unveiled in his hometown Warrington just four days on from breezing past Gerwyn Price to win yet another title in Blackpool.

The teen darts sensation signed his name on the artwork, took time to pose with fans for photos and played darts in front of the crowd present.

However he is still keeping himself grounded, both mentally and physically.

"[The mural is] very good," Littler said. "I actually saw it yesterday or the day before. I didn't want to see it, but they've done a really good job.

"I'm really happy. Someone said you can see it from miles away. It's that big, it's that tall.

"At first, they wanted me to sit on the roof. I said no chance! I'll just stand on the pavement."

articles.title: Commonwealth Games: England fight back to beat South Africa and reach netball semi-finals at Glasgow 2026
articles.summary: In a winner-takes-all group match to progress to the semi-finals, England came out on top against South Africa to secure a place in the last four; England overcame an early deficit to maintain their 100 per cent record of reaching the semi-finals at the Commonwealth Games
articles.body:
England fought back to beat South Africa 58-54 to reach the netball semi-finals at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

Both sides needed to win to book a spot in the last four and England roared back from an early 17-11 deficit after the first quarter to keep their hopes of a second Commonwealth gold alive.

The Vitality Roses will face New Zealand in the second of Saturday's semi-finals after Australia play Jamaica, then the gold and bronze-medal matches take place on Sunday.

"Shout out to Halimat Adio. She was unreal in that second quarter. So proud of her to bring us that energy and get us back in the game when we needed it," captain Francesca Williams told TNT Sports.

"We have been under pressure all week to perform so for us to finish out a game like that and ride the wave of goal for goal in the last quarter and come out on top, I'm so proud."

England got off to a nervy start as South Africa goal shooter Elmere van der Berg came flying out of the blocks with 16 goals from 19 attempts which silenced the crowd at the OVO Hydro.

Halimat Adio and Funmi Fadoju came on, which tightened up England's defence, and it changed the momentum of the match as they slowly got themselves back into the contest to trail just 29-28 at half-time.

England went on a charge early in the third quarter with five consecutive goals to move 35-30 ahead and took a 45-41 lead into the last quarter.

As the clock ran down, England calmly maintained their slender four-goal advantage as Olivia Tchine and Lois Pearson kept their composure up front to get Anna Stembridge's side over the line.

Stembridge stepped up to become head coach just four months before the Commonwealth Games after Jess Thirlby resigned.

articles.title: Commonwealth Games: Tuvalu boxer wins country's first medal without winning a single fight
articles.summary: Tarona Taafaki has claimed the Pacific Ocean island's first ever medal at the Commonwealth Games; the 20-year-old took on India's Lovlina Borgohain in Glasgow on Friday night
articles.body:
Boxer Tarona Taafaki has won Tuvalu their first ever Commonwealth Games medal as she took bronze in the women's 75kg boxing division.

The 20-year-old lost her semi-final bout, falling to defeat against India's Lovlina Borgohain on Friday night after judges unanimously scored every round against her - however Taafaki still picked up a medal.

She reached the semi-final via a bye, and with only five entrants in her category and Commonwealth Games rules ensuring each semi-finalist receive a bronze medal, the boxer instantly made history for her country.

Her coach and father Badi Taafaki told the Press Association: "For the people of Tuvalu, this medal means everything.

"We're one of the smallest nations in the world, so a medal like this is hugely significant. We have worked so hard to get here. For me as a coach, it's a stepping stone."

Tuvalu, a tiny island in the Pacific Ocean, is the fourth-smallest nation in the world.

"When I was growing up, boxing barely existed in Tuvalu," said Badi. "We didn't have gloves, so we were forced to fight bare-knuckle, and hit bags filled with sand."

Athletes even train on the island's airport runway, as it's the most stable stretch of land amid the effects of climate change.

"Yes, we train on the airport runway," Badi said. "When a plane comes in, everyone moves aside. As soon as it leaves, we go back on the tarmac, because there is nowhere else to train.

"If we can win medals, more people around the world will recognise Tuvalu and begin to understand the challenges we face because of climate change.

"It is very real for us. The coastal erosion is unbelievable, and the countdown is now measured in years, not decades.

"Some islands have lost half their land. At high tide the sea comes right through. People living on the coast can't sleep if there's a storm, because the waves can come straight through their homes."

Taafaki is not the first boxer to win a Commonwealth Games medal without winning a fight.

Australia's Taylah Robertson won bronze in the women's flyweight category in 2018 despite losing her bout to England's Lisa Whiteside.

Taafaki's opponent Borgohain will now face Emma-Sue Greentree of Australia in the final.

articles.title: Commonwealth Games - Australia 68-50 England: Roses suffer comprehensive defeat to Diamonds in netball bronze-medal match
articles.summary: Australia inflict comprehensive 68-50 defeat on England in the Commonwealth Games bronze-medal match; England leave the Games without a medal as Australia make it seven straight Commonwealth Games campaigns with a medal; New Zealand beat Jamaica in gold-medal match
articles.body:
England leave the Commonwealth Games without a medal in netball after suffering a comprehensive 68-50 defeat to Australia at the Hydro in Glasgow.

The Vitality Roses never really got going against a team who had already handed them a damaging defeat in the pool stage of the tournament, and a 19-10 Diamonds lead at the end of the first quarter proved to be unassailable for Anna Stembridge's side.

Australia, on the other hand, regain some pride by winning the bronze after their 46-45 defeat to Jamaica in their semi-final, meaning they extend their record of winning a medal in netball at each of the seven Commonwealth Games since the sport was introduced in 1998.

Jamaica have taken home silver, with New Zealand finally reigning supreme with a 56-48 win in the gold-medal contest.

"It was just so tough," England captain Fran Williams told TNT Sport. "When you come off the back with such a short turnaround to play in a game where you would be rather playing [the gold-medal match] later on is really hard.

"I was really proud of the way we showed up at the start and we just showed we weren't able to hold onto that with how the score blew out.

"We are gutted with that. Really disappointed."

The Roses - who arguably exceeded expectations after a turbulent build-up to the tournament including the departure of their head coach Jess Thirlby in March - got off to a fast start, managing to tie 9-9 with Australia in the first quarter, but the Roses scored just two more goals for the Diamonds' next 10 as the reigning Commonwealth champions started to establish a lead.

A 35-24 half-time deficit left England with a chance of getting back into the game, but Sophie Garbin's hat-trick for Australia towards the end of the period left a hefty lead of 13 for Stembridge's side to overturn, and a deflating fourth-quarter from England allowed the Diamonds to extend their lead to 18 and secure the bronze.

"Yesterday was a really tough day for the whole group," Australia captain Liz Watson told TNT Sports. "The way we came out and responded and have a really good performance and make a statement.

"We're disappointed about how we finished up with the bronze but we know how hard international netball is at the moment.

"We love to put on this dress, we have such a rich history of success with the Diamonds and we pride ourselves on doing that and wanting to be better."
